variants.name: Anxious tech skeptics, wary of others
variants.text: These respondents combine guarded trust in people with low confidence in institutions and mounting unease about automation. They tend to rate robots and AI as uncomfortable or worrying, while still holding a generally satisfied view of how democracy works. Their answers on social trust, institutional trust, and technology cluster together, forming a cautious, skeptical outlook that is not outright pessimistic about daily life.

variants.name: Content middle-class, routine-leaning family people
variants.text: These respondents describe their finances as stable, their life as fairly routine, and their happiness as high, with family and social contact fairly frequent. Views on the economy and taxes often run negative while personal finances feel steady, so they separate private contentment from public gloom. Their answers on social life, work-family tension, and personal satisfaction move together, showing a settled, family-centred orientation.

variants.name: Politically detached yet trusting realists
variants.text: These respondents show low to moderate political interest and mixed satisfaction with democratic processes, while often verifying political information online. Their trust in others and their views on technology lean toward the middle or mildly positive, with few extreme ratings. Answers on civic engagement, economic outlook, and emerging technology tend to hover around neutral, producing a measured but noncommittal profile.

variant_stats.name: Anxious tech skeptics, wary of others

variants.name: Distrustful, financially strained, disengaged
variants.text: Respondents describe a cluster of low institutional trust, deep dissatisfaction with how democracy and the economy are running, and a sense that their own finances have worsened. Political interest is minimal, and life feels routine or dull rather than fulfilling. Answers move together: those who feel financially squeezed also tend to rate the national economy harshly, want less income tax, and show little engagement with political news or institutions.

variants.name: Stable social life, wary of change
variants.text: These people combine a fairly ordinary, low-stakes social routine with a skeptical outlook. They maintain frequent contact with relatives or close circles, yet express pessimism about the broader economy and institutions. Attitudes toward technology and automation tend to be mixed or cautious, and they lean toward wanting more public investment in science while still feeling uneasy about robots and AI taking over human tasks.

variants.name: Cautious about technology and tasks
variants.text: The defining tendency is a split between everyday life and emerging technology. Respondents are comfortable with some technological tools yet express worry about artificial intelligence and are reluctant to hand over human activities to machines. Their views on family, work, and scientific funding are moderate or uncertain, and they often hover near the middle of scales rather than committing to strong positions, with little enthusiasm for expanding automation.

variant_stats.name: Stable social life, wary of change

variants.name: Content with personal finances
variants.text: Respondents report feeling financially secure and improving over recent years, rating their household income as average or above while expressing a sense of personal well-being. Their general happiness is high even when their view of national conditions and democracy is mixed or negative. Their social lives are modest, with occasional rather than frequent evenings out, and they lean toward thinking taxes are too high and science underfunded.

variants.name: Affluent but skeptical of institutions
variants.text: These people see themselves as comfortably off or upper class and feel their financial situation has been getting better, yet they distrust many public institutions and are dissatisfied with how democracy works. They tend to rate national conditions poorly while personally feeling fine, and they check political information online carefully. Their daily life feels routine, with social contact mostly limited to relatives or infrequent outings.

variants.name: Trusting, engaged, mixed outlook
variants.text: Respondents combine general interpersonal trust with a moderate, mixed view of institutions and technology, neither strongly enthusiastic nor alarmed. They are engaged with politics and actively verify news, and their satisfaction with democracy ranges from fair to low depending on the person. Social life is regular with relatives and sometimes friends, and attitudes toward automation and AI sit in the middle, with mild concern and partial comfort.

variants.name: Politically engaged, distrustful of institutions
variants.text: Respondents are highly interested in politics and check claims carefully online, yet are dissatisfied with how democracy works. They trust people broadly but give institutions sharply varying levels of trust, with some extremes, and they lean toward feeling that taxes are too low and that the economy is doing well. Their answers tend to pair strong civic attention with skepticism about formal systems.

variants.name: Stable mood, routine social life
variants.text: Respondents report being very happy even while describing life as dull and their financial situations as modest or below average. Their social lives are either frequent and local or sparse, and they tend to hold strong views on family and work roles. Answers reflect contentment and low novelty-seeking rather than strong excitement, with opinions on economic conditions that run against their personal circumstances.

variants.name: Divided views on technology and work
variants.text: Respondents combine high anxiety about robots and artificial intelligence with strong agreement or disagreement on technology statements that do not consistently line up. Their support for scientific research and their views on how family life suffers from work tend to move together, pointing to a pattern of pronounced opinions that shift between extremes depending on the topic. They express worry about automation alongside a sense that public spending on research is either just right or clearly insufficient.

variant_stats.name: Divided views on technology and work

variants.name: Disillusioned, financially strained, disengaged
variants.text: Respondents express broad distrust of institutions and of how democracy works, feel their finances have slipped below average, and rate the economy poorly. They describe their lives as routine or dull and their overall mood as not too happy, while showing little interest in politics. Their social lives are thin, with rare evenings out and infrequent time with relatives. Views on technology and AI are wary, and they favour more spending on science.

variants.name: Withdrawn, low-trust, socially isolated
variants.text: The dominant tendency is withdrawal: low interest in politics, low trust in institutions and other people, and little time spent socially with friends or family. Financial satisfaction is low, though some respondents feel their situation is stable or improving. Life is described as dull or routine rather than exciting, and happiness is modest. Attitudes toward robots and AI are uneasy, while the desire for more public spending on research is consistent.

variants.name: Economically pessimistic but tax-tolerant
variants.text: Economic judgement is harsh: the economy is seen as bad, personal finances are below average, and satisfaction with money is minimal. Yet these respondents do not want higher taxes, treating their current burden as about right or too low. Politically they are dissatisfied and uninvolved, and they report not being very happy. Their outlook on technology splits into strong discomfort with automation alongside support for scientific funding.
